claims.text: The target alloy is equiatomic Hf–Mo–Nb–Ta–Ti, corresponding to approximately 20 at% of each element.
The as-synthesized Hf–Mo–Nb–Ta–Ti alloy is a well-mixed, single-phase refractory solid solution.
The Hf–Mo–Nb–Ta–Ti alloy exhibits bulk superconductivity at ambient pressure.
Diamond-anvil-cell four-probe transport measurements can track superconductivity under pressure.
Magnetic susceptibility can be measured concurrently under pressure to confirm bulk superconductivity.
In situ high-pressure X-ray diffraction can be used in the proposed experiment to monitor lattice parameters and phase purity.
The relevant experimental window extends from ambient pressure to about 100 GPa and down to 1.8 K.
Hydrostatic pressure reduces the alloy's lattice parameters and interatomic distances.
Reduced interatomic distances enhance d-orbital overlap.
Pressure-induced changes in d-orbital overlap alter the electron–phonon coupling strength.
Pressure-induced changes in d-orbital overlap shift the density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in electron–phonon coupling and the Fermi-level density of states change the superconducting gap and Tc in a manner consistent with BCS theory for disordered superconductors.
Increasing pressure will produce a systematic, measurable change in Tc relative to its ambient-pressure value.
Increasing pressure will produce a systematic, measurable change in the upper critical field Hc2.
The pressure-induced change in Tc may be either an enhancement or a suppression.
Deviations from classic BCS predictions under pressure may indicate additional complexity or an alternative pairing mechanism.
The as-synthesized alloy at ambient pressure provides the control baseline for Tc and Hc2.
The hypothesis applies only while the material remains a single-phase high-entropy solid solution without phase separation or unintended structural transitions.
A Tc shift without a corresponding lattice-parameter change would falsify lattice compression as the sole governing cause.
Phase separation coincident with a change in Tc would falsify the proposed lattice-compression mechanism.

contradictions.description: The boundary declares phase separation and unintended structural transitions outside the hypothesis's domain, whereas the falsification rule treats phase separation coincident with a Tc change as a falsifying result. An out-of-boundary event should invalidate the test rather than directly falsify the bounded hypothesis.

The hypothesis says lattice compression is the primary control, but the falsification rule tests the stronger claim that superconductivity is governed solely by lattice compression. Refuting exclusivity would not necessarily refute primary control.
